owner_name: Simon Sadler (via Blackpool Football Club Stadium and Property Ltd, inc. May 2019)
note: When Simon Sadler bought 96.2% of Blackpool FC from the receivers in June 2019 he separately bought the stadium, stadium property and training ground in a personal capacity; a separate company, Blackpool Football Club Stadium and Property Ltd, was set up in May 2019. It is not confirmed whether that company sits under the club company, so the ground may not pass automatically with the club.

lease_note: Rolling 7-year lease at a peppercorn rent (as reported)
note: The club bought the ground in 1933 and sold it to Luton Borough Council in 1989, leasing it back since. The club plans to move to a new 25,000-seat stadium at Power Court, approved December 2024, with piling under way by February 2026 and a target opening for 2028-29.

The council took the stadium back in 1980 and installed the club as tenant; the club rents it from the council and the two have jointly funded stand upgrades. There have been disputes over rent increases and funding for the North Stand, but no change of ownership found.

In December 2018 the club bought the freehold of the ground from Hyndburn Council for £400,000, ending about 50 years of leasing the land (it already owned the buildings). Owner Andy Holt put the club up for sale in October 2023 and an investment deal was reported later; no change to the ground's ownership was found.

Stadium references list the club as owner of Gresty Road, its home since 1906. A sale of a controlling stake was reported, but no transfer of the ground away from the club was found; freehold detail not confirmed from filings.

Stadium references list the club as owner of Blundell Park, its home since 1899. The 1878 Partners consortium (Jason Stockwood) bought the club from John Fenty in 2021 and has said a stadium move is not an immediate priority; earlier new-stadium plans involved council-owned land.

lease_note: Club holds a lease; terms not found
note: Sources conflict: stadium reference sites list Salford City FC as owner, but Place North West's 2024 coverage of the proposed AJ Bell Stadium swap (Salford Red Devils to take a lease at Moor Lane) describes the Peninsula Stadium as council-owned. The newer, more specific report is preferred; the club funded the rebuild of all four stands.

lease_note: Club is a tenant under a lease agreed with the council before the 2021 move; term not found
note: The £44m stadium opened in 2021, is owned by City of York Council and shared with York Knights and York Valkyrie rugby league. The club had to settle lease differences with the council before moving in from Bootham Crescent in January 2021.

Stadium references list Carlisle United as owner of Brunton Park, its home since 1909. The Piatak family's Castle Sports Group bought 90% of CUFC Holdings in November 2023 and is spending over £4.5m on the ground; no separate property company or lease was found.

The stadium and the wider Mill Farm sports village, opened in 2016, are owned by Tangerine Holdings, the Haythornthwaite family company; David Haythornthwaite also controls the club. It was not confirmed whether the club company sits inside the same group, so the ground may not pass automatically with the club.

lease_note: Existing lease said by the club to secure at least another 20 years at Aggborough
note: Wyre Forest District Council holds the freehold; in January 2026 its cabinet considered selling the freehold of the ground, car park and social club to the club, with covenants to keep it a football ground. Negotiations were still ongoing in 2026 and no completed sale was found.

Bob Andrews and Steve Lathbury sold their majority stake to Abdullah Ashraf's Dawn Group International, and Ashraf promised to buy the Lamb Ground. Tamworth Borough Council said any sale of the council land would need valuation and cabinet approval and no terms had been agreed; no completed sale or active dispute was found.

owner_name: Private consortium that bought the ground c.2014 (name not found)
note: Facing debts around 2014, the members voted unanimously to sell the ground to one of two consortiums, with the club continuing as a members club playing at Testwood. The buyer's identity and lease terms were not found; Snows Motor Group is the naming-rights sponsor and its chairman Stephen Snow chairs the club.

The club has said it hopes to sell Cressing Road, its home since 1923 (built by the Crittall Windows Company), to fund a new ground, which implies the club holds it. One reference site lists the shareholders L Harding, K Cowell/Cowell & Cooper Ltd and V Dixon as 'owners', which appears to describe the club, not the land; freehold not confirmed.

lease_note: Lease granted to the new club in May 2010; term not found
note: Researched Chester FC, the phoenix formed in 2010 after Chester City was wound up. The council owns the Deva Stadium, which straddles the England-Wales border, and granted its lease to the fans' group behind Chester FC in May 2010.

lease_note: Surrey County FA holds the head lease; the club plays there under it. In 2026 the club and Surrey FA proposed a new leasing arrangement.
note: Mole Valley District Council has owned the rebuilt Meadowbank facilities since they opened in 2018, with Surrey County FA as leaseholder and Dorking Wanderers playing their home games there. In 2026 the council said it will not sell the freehold but will consider a new lease.

lease_note: Reversionary 15-year lease agreed July 2021, running to 2036
note: The Cheriton Road sports complex is owned by Folkestone & Hythe District Council and operated by the Cheriton Road Sports Ground Trust. In 2021 the club signed a reversionary 15-year lease with the council, securing tenure to 2036.

owner_name: Craig and Amanda Gwilt (held separately from the club)
note: Keys Park was owned by former chairman Steve Price separately from the club, which he sold to Graham Jones and Hayden Dando in 2020. In early 2024 Craig and Amanda Gwilt bought both the club and Keys Park from Price; the reports do not say whether the ground was then put into the club company.

owner_name: Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk
lease_note: 25-year lease from 1 February 2010 granted to Buster Chapman's new club; rent set at 2% of gross receipts
note: After King's Lynn FC folded in 2009, the council granted a 25-year lease on the council-owned Walks to the new club (Lynn FC, now King's Lynn Town) from February 2010. No later change of ownership was found.

Stadium references list Marine AFC as owner of Rossett Park, its home since 1904. In 2025 the club unveiled plans for a new stadium in Kirkby (Knowsley) as part of a housing scheme; tenure of Rossett Park not confirmed from a primary source.
The club has played at Stainton Park (Red Bank, Pilkington Road) since 1970, after leaving land leased from the Earl of Wilton. Two searches found no source on who holds the freehold today.

owner_name: Bought in 2015 by Geoff Thompson's regime from John Rundle; holding entity (club or Thompson) not confirmed
note: The club was homeless from 2013 after its Filtrona Park lease ended; in 2015 new chairman Geoff Thompson bought the ground from John Rundle and renamed it Mariners Park. An ORY Investment-led consortium took a majority stake from 29 May 2026 with Thompson staying as chairman and shareholder; no source says whether the ground sits in the club company or with Thompson.

lease_note: Reversionary lease granted in 2022 extending tenure to 2034; talks on a longer lease continuing
note: The council built Longmead in 1980 and gave it to the club as compensation after redeveloping the old Angel Ground. In 2022 the council extended the club's lease to 2034 alongside approval for a 3G pitch.

The club held Woodspring Park on a council lease extended to 99 years, then sold that land to Barratt, splitting proceeds 50/50 with the council, and moved in 2004 to the new Woodspring Stadium, which the club owns. Freehold of the new site not confirmed from a primary source.

lease_note: Year-to-year tenancy; the club owns the car park and gets a 20% share of any sale profit
note: The club are tenants at Lye Meadow, owning only the car park. Bromsgrove planners backed 25 homes on Lye Meadow with a seven-figure contribution to a new stadium at The Hayes; the club rejected a groundshare and stays at Lye Meadow for one final season in 2026-27.

The club sold its old Mill Field ground to developers to fund the move to the purpose-built Parkside, which opened in 2016-17. Reference sites list the club as owner; freehold not confirmed from a primary source.

lease_note: Council cabinet proposal for Hampshire FA to surrender its lease and the club to get a new long-term lease directly, with Hampshire FA subleasing part of the site; completion not confirmed
note: After eviction from the Camrose in 2019 and a groundshare at Winchester, the reformed Basingstoke Town Community FC returned to the council-owned Winklebury complex, then leased to Hampshire FA. The council has since moved to grant the club its own long-term lease.

ground: Bottom Meadow (The SB Stadium), Sandhurst Memorial Park
owner_name: Public land in Sandhurst Memorial Park (freeholder believed to be Sandhurst Town Council; not confirmed); lease/operation by SB Group
lease_note: Ground was sublet from Sandhurst Town FC; SB Group (Kayne Steinborn-Busse) announced a lease in 2023 and regained operational control for 2025-26
note: Bracknell Town left Larges Lane (home since 1933) in June 2021 to groundshare with Sandhurst Town at Bottom Meadow, after SB Group spent about £2m upgrading it; the club keeps its headquarters at Larges Lane. Bottom Meadow is part of Sandhurst Memorial Park and was built in 1997 with Bracknell Forest and Sandhurst Town Council support; the freeholder was not confirmed.

owner_name: Gigg Lane Stadium Ltd (within the fan-owned Bury FC society group)
note: After the original Bury FC was expelled from the EFL in 2019, the fans' group Est.1885 bought Gigg Lane from the administrator in February 2022 (with £1m government help) through Gigg Lane Stadium Ltd. That society merged with the Bury AFC society in May 2023 and the club returned to Gigg Lane as Bury FC in 2023-24.
The club has played at Alwyns Lane since 1926 on land donated by Sir Edward Stern as a football ground for the parish's premier club. Two searches found no source on who holds the freehold today.

The club took over the Linden Homes sports and social club in 2011 when it faced closure, and later returned there from Bradley with new floodlights and stands. Sources say it 'took over' the club but not whether it bought the freehold or holds a lease.

lease_note: Planned new 4,000-capacity stadium to be leased to the club for 125 years
note: Property firm Meadow bought the Champion Hill site in 2014; in 2018 a dispute saw the club locked out and groundsharing at Tooting & Mitcham while Southwark Council threatened a compulsory purchase. The club and Meadow later submitted a joint scheme, and in December 2025 Southwark approved the land arrangements for a new stadium plus 219 homes, with the stadium leased to the club for 125 years.

ground: Jubilee Stadium (The Spiers & Hartwell Stadium), Cheltenham Road
owner_name: Wychavon District Council and Worcestershire County Council (reported)
note: The club sold its Common Road ground for housing in 2006, groundshared with Worcester City, and opened the new Jubilee Stadium in 2012. A Pitchcare feature says the club maintains the pitches on the site for Wychavon District Council and Worcestershire County Council, who own it; no lease details found.

owner_name: Eamonn McGurk and Alex Petheram (club co-owners/co-chairmen)
note: Meadow Park was destroyed by floods in 2007; the club spent 13 years in exile before a £4m rebuild, raised 3.5m, reopened in late 2020. Reference sources name co-chairmen Eamonn McGurk and Alex Petheram as the stadium's owners rather than the club company; whether the ground would pass with the club is not confirmed.
The club has played at Reynolds Field, Perivale (beside Perivale Park, London Borough of Ealing) since 1981. Two searches found no source on who holds the freehold.

lease_note: 2015 council report proposed surrendering the 125-year lease of 1995 for up to £125k and granting a 25-year lease with a rolling mutual break, outside the 1954 Act; end year assumes completion c.2015
note: Hyde sold Ewen Fields to Tameside Council in 1986 so an artificial pitch could be laid; the club owns the buildings on site. A November 2015 council report proposed replacing the club's 125-year lease (1995) with a 25-year lease with a rolling mutual break.

owner_name: Mole Valley District Council (inferred, not confirmed)
lease_note: Club reported to hold a 25-year lease (date not found)
note: Leatherhead have played at Fetcham Grove, next to the council's leisure centre, since 1946. An old Get Surrey report on Dorking FC's lease talks with Mole Valley council cites Leatherhead's 25-year lease as a comparison, implying the council is landlord; no direct statement of the freeholder was found.

owner_name: Lewes District Council, as sole trustee of the Mountfield Pleasure Ground Trust (charity)
lease_note: New 25-year lease agreed c.2024 to replace a lease ending in 2025; exact end year not confirmed
note: The Dripping Pan is held by the Mountfield Pleasure Ground Trust, a charity whose sole trustee is Lewes District Council, so it could also be read as 'landlord (charity)'. With its old lease ending in 2025, the fan-owned club got a longer 25-year lease so it could bid for ground-improvement grants.

lease_note: Lease extended by 17 years, leaving 53 years to run, to 2057
note: The club holds a long lease from Peterborough City Council, which was extended by 17 years to run until 2057 ahead of plans for a new clubhouse and more capacity.

lease_note: 21-year lease issued after a court order following a lease dispute c.2009-2011; later renewals not found
note: Townsend Meadow is part of St Mary's Lands, owned by Warwick District Council and governed by the St Mary's Lands Act 1984. After a dispute in which the council admitted it had 'granted this lease twice', a 21-year lease was issued in line with a court order; the ground has since had a new 3G pitch and clubhouse work.

lease_note: 30-year lease granted 2016 at a concessionary £2,000 a year, tied to a community 3G pitch project
note: The council owns the land and in 2016 granted the club a new 30-year lease to 2046 at a concessionary rent to support a community 3G pitch. A later Redditch Standard report described a rent row casting doubt over the club's future; no change in ownership found.

ground: Zeeco Stadium (Borderville Sports Centre), Ryhall Road
owner_name: Burghley Estate (freeholder); facility shared with New College Stamford
lease_note: Land leased from the Burghley Estate for the joint college/club development; terms not found
note: Stamford AFC left Wothorpe Road in November 2014 for the new Borderville sports complex, built in partnership with New College Stamford on land provided by the Burghley Estate. Burghley owns the land, which was leased for the development; who holds the head lease (college or club) was not confirmed.
The club moved to Wordsworth Drive in 1953 on a lease from Taunton Borough Council and bought the ground from the council in the 1970s (exact year not found). No later sale found.

Reference sites list the club as owner of Cantilever Park, its home since 1956, which has since been renamed the Cal.Delivery Stadium under a sponsorship deal. No lease or third-party landlord was found, but the freehold was not confirmed from a primary source.

The club moved to the new New Cuthbury ground in December 2020, renamed the Wyatt Homes Stadium in July 2024; earlier Dorset planning papers showed the old Cuthbury site being folded into a housing proposal. Two searches found no source on who holds the freehold of the new ground.
The club moved from Sunnyside Lane to Lodge Road in 1984, building a 236-seat stand in 1987 and adding floodlights in 1988. Two searches found no source on who holds the freehold.
